title: API Versioning and Documentation
description: Learn how to version ASP.NET Core APIs so you can evolve your endpoints without breaking existing clients. Explore URL segment, query string, and header-based versioning strategies, and understand how to document your API for other developers.

blocks.text: APIs evolve. New features get added, old ones get deprecated, and data shapes change. Without versioning, every change breaks existing clients. API versioning lets you ship new versions of an endpoint while keeping the old version running for clients that have not migrated yet.

ASP.NET Core does not include versioning in the box, but the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Versioning NuGet package provides a clean, convention-based approach. Versioning can be expressed through the URL, query string, or request headers — each with trade-offs.
Why Version an API?

Versioning lets you change the contract of an API without forcing all consumers to update simultaneously. A mobile app with a slow rollout might still call version 1 of an endpoint months after version 2 has shipped. Without versioning, you would have to keep every change backward-compatible indefinitely, which becomes impossible for any non-trivial API.
When to Introduce a New Version

Create a new version when you change the shape of a response, remove a field, rename an endpoint, or change required behavior in a way that breaks existing clients. Minor additions that are backward-compatible — such as adding an optional field — do not require a new version.
Versioning Strategies

The three most common versioning strategies are URL segment versioning, query string versioning, and header-based versioning. Each has different implications for how clients call your API and how you manage routes.
URL Segment Versioning

The version number appears directly in the URL path: /api/v1/products and /api/v2/products. This is the most visible strategy because the version is part of the address. It is also the easiest for clients to test manually. The downside is that URLs change between versions, which some purists argue violates REST principles.
Query String Versioning

The version is passed as a query parameter: /api/products?api-version=2.0. The base URL stays the same across versions. This keeps routes cleaner but makes the version less visible in logs and debugging tools. It is also easy for clients to forget the parameter.
Header-Based Versioning

The version is sent in a custom request header, such as X-Api-Version: 2. URLs never change. This is the most RESTful approach from a pure URI design perspective, but it is the hardest for developers to test manually — they need a tool that lets them set custom headers rather than just typing a URL.

blocks.title: Start with URL Segment Versioning
blocks.text: URL segment versioning (e.g., /api/v1/products) is the most widely adopted strategy. It is immediately visible in logs, browser history, and debugging tools. You can switch to header-based versioning later if your API matures to that level of sophistication.
Implementing Versioning with the Versioning Package

Install the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Versioning package and register it in Program.cs. You then apply the [ApiVersion] attribute to controllers and optionally use [MapToApiVersion] on individual actions when a controller serves multiple versions.

blocks.text: API Documentation Practices

Good documentation tells other developers what your API does, how to call it, what parameters it expects, and what it returns. Documentation is not a one-time task — it must stay current as the API changes. A documented API with versioning is much easier to maintain than one with a wiki page that gets out of sync.

blocks.title: What Every API Endpoint Should Document
items: HTTP method and full URL path with any required parameters
Request body schema (field names, types, required vs optional)
Success response: status code, response body schema, and example payload
Error responses: which status codes can be returned and what they mean
Authentication requirements (if any endpoint needs a token or role)
Rate limiting or throttling rules that apply to the endpoint

blocks.text: Deprecating an API Version

When you are ready to retire an old version, add a Deprecated flag to the version declaration. The versioning library will include this in response headers, signaling to clients that they should migrate. Set a clear deprecation date and communicate it to consumers well in advance.

blocks.title: Key Terms: API Versioning and Documentation

terms.definition: The practice of maintaining multiple versions of an API so changes do not break existing consumers.
Version expressed in the URL path (e.g., /api/v1/products). Most visible and widely adopted strategy.
A version marked as deprecated signals to clients that it will be removed and they should migrate.
The component that determines which version a client is requesting, reading from URL, query string, or headers.
An attribute that restricts an action method to only respond to requests for a specific API version.

blocks.title: Versioning Is Not Free
blocks.text: Every version you maintain is code you must test, document, and secure. Avoid creating versions for trivial changes. Only version when you have a breaking change that cannot be handled with optional fields or feature flags.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: API Versioning and Documentation
points: API versioning lets you evolve endpoints without breaking existing clients
URL segment versioning puts the version in the path — /api/v1/products — and is the most common approach
Query string and header versioning keep URLs stable but are less visible for debugging
Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Versioning handles version resolution and deprecation signaling
The [Deprecated = true] flag adds response headers that tell clients to migrate
Good documentation includes request/response schemas, error codes, and authentication requirements
blocks.takeaway: Versioning is an investment in your API's longevity. Plan for it from the start, choose a strategy your team can maintain, and deprecate old versions deliberately with clear timelines rather than letting them accumulate indefinitely.

blocks.title: Exercise: Add Versioning to an Existing API
blocks.description: Take an existing unversioned API controller and add versioning support following best practices.
steps: Add the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Versioning NuGet package to your project
Register AddApiVersioning in Program.cs with ReportApiVersions enabled
Update the route template to include v{version:apiVersion} in the path
Create a V2 DTO that adds two new optional fields not present in V1
Add a MapToApiVersion("2.0") action that returns the new DTO
Test both /api/v1/products and /api/v2/products return different payloads
blocks.expectedOutcome: Two versions of the same endpoint responding at different URLs with different DTO shapes. The API-Supported-Versions response header should list both versions, and calling v1 should return the original shape.
